comments.text:
Canada spent decades trying to get rid of Ripple Rock, and at one point, people even suggested using an atomic bomb. 😳

Do you think blowing it up was the only realistic solution, or would you have left it alone and kept ships timing the tides?

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Yeah, that proposal is one of the strangest parts of the whole story. Ripple Rock was already sitting in an extremely dangerous, turbulent shipping channel, yet some planners seriously considered using it as a bridge support instead of removing it. Thankfully that idea never went ahead.

comments.author: @WillardWallace-y5g
comments.text:
Oh wow! They showed this on 8mm in school when I was in 5th grade! This was a big deal bcuz in indigineous culture in the 70s & 80s, there r some serious legends about that place. Like how even whales would avoid it. Or during salmon season, u could only fish it at slack tide for 15 minutes b4 it sucked ur boat thru. We had elder indigineous speakers come to our highschool who saw the rock take out boats, & then saw the rock removed. They told us how it changed the ecosystem in the years after. There were whales, & salmon using the passage, also sea lions. They were never there b4, but they showed up.

The indigineous ppls in that place didnt like ripple rock. It had caused a lot of funerals. The sad part was,  as traffic increased, they got to watch a whole lot more ppl die unnecessarily. They had no way of dealing with the rock, & had been putting up with it for so long, they were glad to see it gone. The one women who spoke, lost her husband during a crossing after getting sucked thru. Ripple rock was not done with her, it took her oldest son the same way several years l8r. She said in the days b4, every single person in her band had either lost someone personally, or had known someone who had been lost.

I dont know if they still do it, but there was a remembrance dance for the lost at their pow-wows.    

It was pretty cool to see it from their side. Luckily, I wasnt sick or injured that day, so I was in attendance, & got to b part of the oral tradition.👍

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: This is an incredible piece of local history, thank you for taking the time to share it. I came across the Ligʷiłdaxʷ history of Mətane while researching the video, but not these personal stories about the losses, the elders who remembered it, or what people noticed in the years after the rock was removed. Hearing that you were taught this directly by elders adds a completely different side to the story. I’m really glad you shared it here.

comments.text: Why is everything "QUIETLY" now.   Even things that can't be LOUD? It's just dousing meaningful words with meaningless ones. How is this useful?

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Fair point on “quietly ironic”, I could’ve left the word out there. Later in the video, though, “quietly” was meant as “outside public attention,” referring to British officials using the Ripple Rock data in later detection research revealed through declassified files. But I agree the word gets overused in narration these days. Appreciate you calling it out.

comments.author: @davidk7544
comments.text: This was an incredible feat. And completely successful. Canadian Engineering at its best. How they did this without laser levels and radio telemetry is.... just so impressive.  I must say the local indigenous were *superb* humanitarians. Excellent people. As usual the US could go suck an egg.  Bringing up the Reynolds number showed competence, I appreciate that.  The folks wanting to let the taller ripple rock be used as a support for a train bridge is unimaginable.  That would require a coffer dam that technology of that era simply could not be built that would withstand such turbulence.  I agree, the only way removing this bit of rock was from underneath.  The US did something similar in the waters off NYC.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Really appreciate this comment. The engineering behind Ripple Rock was incredible, especially considering the technology they were working with at the time. The underwater drilling and monitoring made the whole project even more impressive to me. And yes, the idea of trying to build around the rock instead of removing it shows just how difficult the problem really was. Thanks for watching and adding all that context.
